blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights the paper's central insight: traditional block-level I/O schedulers lack high-level context for effective write-reordering and accounting, while system-call level schedulers have the context but lack low-level knowledge. The authors propose 'split-level IO scheduling,' a framework that intercepts at both levels to combine their strengths. By implementing handlers at system-call, page-cache, and block layers, the framework enables accurate process tracking, cost estimation, and prevention of filesystem-imposed orderings that conflict with scheduling goals. The paper demonstrates three split-level schedulers: AFQ (fair queuing with 28x fewer priority misallocations than Linux CFQ), Split-Deadline (reducing tail latencies by 4x and solving fsync-induced freezes in databases), and Split-Token (improving isolation by 6x and mitigating noisy neighbor problems). The approach is implemented in Linux with ext4 and XFS, showing practical applicability across different filesystems.
paper_abstract: IBM Research-Almaden* built at the block level within an operating system, beneath the file system and just above the device itself. Such block-level schedulers are given a stream of requests and are thus faced with the question: which requests should be dispatched, and when, in order to achieve the goals of the system? We introduce split-level I/O scheduling, a new framework that splits I/O scheduling logic across handlers at three layers of the storage stack: block, system call, and page cache. We demonstrate that traditional block-level I/O schedulers are unable to meet throughput, latency, and isolation goals. By utilizing the split-level framework, we build a variety of novel schedulers to readily achieve these goals: our Actually Fair Queuing scheduler reduces priority-misallocation by 28×; our SplitDeadline scheduler reduces tail latencies by 4×; our Split-Token scheduler reduces sensitivity to interference by 6×. We show that the framework is general and operates correctly with disparate file systems (ext4 and XFS). Finally, we demonstrate that split-level scheduling serves as a useful foundation for databases (SQLite and PostgreSQL), hypervisors (QEMU), and distributed file systems (HDFS), delivering improved isolation and performance in these important application scenarios. Unfortunately, making decisions at the block level is problematic, for two reasons. First, and most importantly, the block-level scheduler fundamentally cannot reorder certain write requests; file systems carefully control write ordering to preserve consistency in the event of system crash or power loss [21, 25]. Second, the blocklevel scheduler cannot perform accurate accounting; the scheduler lacks the requisite information to determine which application was responsible for a particular I/O request.
